one_liner: Blocked, multithreaded meta-compressor (shuffle/bitshuffle plus BloscLZ, LZ4, Zstd, zlib) for typed numeric arrays; can outrun memcpy on compressible data.
what_it_does: Compresses an in-memory buffer of fixed-size elements into a self-describing Blosc 1.x chunk (16-byte header, at most INT_MAX minus 16 bytes per buffer) and back. The API is a codec, not a memcpy replacement: blosc_compress(clevel, doshuffle, typesize, nbytes, src, dest, destsize, ...) and blosc_decompress(src, dest, destsize), thread-safe *_ctx variants that take the codec name, block size and thread count, and blosc_getitem() to pull a range of items out of a compressed buffer without decompressing all of it. It is the engine behind python-blosc, the hdf5-blosc filter and the bloscpack CLI.
how_it_is_fast: The shuffle filter transposes the bytes (bitshuffle: the bits) of each typesize-element so equal-significance bytes sit together, which turns slowly varying numbers into long runs that a fast LZ codec compresses well; x86 gets SSE2/AVX2 kernels chosen at run time by cpuid under pthread_once, other architectures fall back to generic C. The buffer is split into cache-sized blocks (automatic block size up to 256 KB for fast codecs since 1.19) that a worker thread pool shuffles and compresses in cache, the 'blocking technique' of the 2010 CISE 'Starving CPUs' paper. Beating memcpy comes from moving fewer bytes through memory and from using many cores while memcpy uses one.
when_to_use: Low-entropy numeric arrays of 2-8 byte elements (time series, regular grids, sorted ids, sparse data) where shuffle lifts the ratio well above 2x; the README run reached 57x-320x on arange data.
Buffers of roughly 1 MB and up with spare cores: README_THREADED.rst says the thread pool only pays off above 64/128 KB, with a sweet spot near 1 MB per call.
Code or data that must stay on the Blosc 1.x chunk format and C ABI (python-blosc, hdf5-blosc, bloscpack, existing files).
Random access to a slice of items inside a compressed buffer via blosc_getitem().
C89-only toolchains or unusual platforms (README: any C89 compiler; IBM Blue Gene Q A2 reported to work).
when_not_to_use: New projects: the README says c-blosc is in pure maintenance mode with no new features and points to C-Blosc2 (NEON/AltiVec shuffles, AVX512 bitshuffle, super-chunks, frames).

Text, already-compressed or high-entropy bytes, or wrong typesize: without shuffle the README's own run has blosclz at 1.95 GiB/s compress and 2.48 GiB/s decompress at ratio 1.0x, slower than the 2.70 GiB/s memcpy line.
Single-threaded or small-buffer use: the memcpy-beating figures are many-thread runs against a one-thread memmove, and the threaded path falls back to serial below 64/128 KB.

Buffers near 2 GB: BLOSC_MAX_BUFFERSIZE is INT_MAX minus 16, and open issue #385 (Aug 2024, no maintainer reply) reports a Valgrind invalid 8-byte write in fastcopy.c copy_16_bytes and a -1 return when compressing 2,147,483,631 bytes.

Builds with GCC 15 auto-vectorization on some CPUs: open issue #402 (June 2026) reports blosclz+shuffle/bitshuffle tests segfaulting on Cascade Lake and Zen 4 with GCC 15.2.0 -O3 -ftree-vectorize -march=native (workaround -fno-tree-vectorize), root cause unknown.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake); also shipped prebuilt inside python-blosc wheels
integration.dependencies: none required: LZ4 1.10.0, zlib 1.3.1, Zstd 1.5.6 and BloscLZ are bundled in internal-complibs (PREFER_EXTERNAL_* switches to system copies); Snappy is off by default (DEACTIVATE_SNAPPY=ON) because it needs a C++ compiler; pthreads
integration.min_toolchain: C89 C compiler; CMake 3.10+ on main (the v1.21.6 release has open issue #394, failure to build with CMake 4.0)
integration.platforms: any C89 platform; mostly tested on x86 Linux, macOS and Windows and on ARM Linux; SSE2/AVX2 shuffle kernels only on x86 (runtime cpuid dispatch), generic C shuffle elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: blosc_compress/blosc_decompress use one global context behind a global mutex after blosc_init(); for concurrent callers use blosc_compress_ctx/blosc_decompress_ctx exclusively (no blosc_init needed), which start and release their own worker pool on every call when numinternalthreads > 1
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — not a memcpy replacement: it produces a compressed copy that must be decompressed, and only wins over memcpy on compressible typed data with several threads

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the memcpy comparison: the README run (python-blosc 1.5.1.dev0, Blosc 1.11.2) came from the bench/compress_ptr.py of that era (identical at tags v1.5.0 and v1.5.1), which allocates the memmove destination and every decompression destination with np.empty right before timing, so the 0.276 s single-threaded memcpy baseline includes first-touch page faults on 800 MB of fresh memory, while compression writes only the compressed bytes into an oversized uninitialised bytes object (blosc_extension.c v1.5.0 lines 200 and 245) and so faults about 1/57 of the pages at 57x; the np.full pre-fault ('cause page faults here') was only added in v1.9.0. The 6.6x-memcpy compress figure is inflated by the baseline's page-fault cost.

The README run's thread count cannot be reproduced from the published script: the v1.5.x script labels the thread count with blosc.ncores and never calls set_nthreads (python-blosc 1.5.x defaults to min(ncores, 4) threads), yet the pasted output prints 'Detected cores: 56', 'Number of threads to use by default: 4' and then '24 threads', which one run of that script cannot produce; the output came from a locally modified script or was edited, so whether 4 or 24 threads ran is unknown.

blosc_decompress() takes no source length and trusts the compressed size stored in the 16-byte header; for untrusted input call blosc_cbuffer_validate(cbuffer, cbytes, &nbytes) first, which checks the header against the real byte count.

Environment variables silently change the non-ctx calls: BLOSC_NTHREADS, BLOSC_NOLOCK, BLOSC_CLEVEL, BLOSC_SHUFFLE, BLOSC_TYPESIZE, BLOSC_COMPRESSOR and BLOSC_SPLITMODE override the arguments given in code.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick c-blosc over c-blosc2 only when you need the Blosc 1.x format, its frozen C ABI or a C89 compiler; otherwise C-Blosc2 is the maintained successor with ARM SIMD. Over calling LZ4 or Zstd directly, pick Blosc for typed numeric arrays with spare cores (shuffle plus blocking raises both ratio and speed); use plain LZ4/Zstd for text, streams or single-threaded work, and test Stenos if its numbers on your data beat Blosc plus Zstd.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own 2017 run printed in the python-blosc README (Blosc 1.11.2 with BloscLZ 1.0.5, LZ4 1.7.5, Zstd 1.1.2; Xeon E5-2695 v3, CentOS 7.2; C-library compiler flags not given) compresses 10^8 int64/float64 elements (800 MB) at clevel 5 and compares each codec with one ctypes.memmove of the same array: memmove 0.276 s (2.70 GiB/s) versus blosclz+shuffle on arange 17.77 GiB/s compress and 27.18 GiB/s decompress at 57.1x, and lz4+shuffle on randint(0, 1000) data 11.02 / 26.03 GiB/s at 4.5x. Each figure is one time.time() sample, the baseline is one thread against a pool labelled 24 threads, and the baseline time includes page faults on a fresh destination that compression mostly avoids.
status_note: Pure maintenance mode by its own README (last release v1.21.6 on 2024-06-24, last commit 2026-08-27 bumping the CMake minimum, crash issues #385 and #402 open without replies); BSD-3-Clause and easy to vendor, but the published benchmark is a 2017 run on long-superseded codec versions, so re-measure, and prefer C-Blosc2 for new work.
